messages.content: We want to start looking at Maine for next summer. Seven nights for Daniel, Owen, and me, probably Saturday, July 12 through Saturday, July 19. We want Portland and some time farther up the coast. Compare flying from O'Hare into Portland with flying into Boston and driving. Nothing should be booked.

I’ll compare the full door-to-destination time, not just airfare. Before I lay it out, how far up the coast are you considering: Boothbay Harbor, Rockland/Camden, or farther toward Bar Harbor? And are you deciding between one hotel for all seven nights and a Portland/coast split?
Camden or Rockland is far enough. Yes, one base versus a split. We do not need Bar Harbor on this trip.

That keeps the driving manageable. For those dates, the two practical flight structures are: a nonstop ORD-PWM itinerary of roughly 2 hours 25 minutes each way, or one of several ORD-BOS nonstops around 2 hours 20 minutes. PWM has fewer schedules but puts you about 15 minutes from central Portland and roughly 1 hour 45 minutes from Camden. BOS offers more flight choices, but the rental pickup and drive materially extend the arrival day. What departure window should I use for a fair comparison?
Use a morning departure, but not the first flight of the day. Assume we can leave O'Hare between 8:00 and 10:00.

In that window, a representative PWM structure is an ORD departure around 8:30-9:15 a.m., arriving about noon Eastern. Allowing 45-60 minutes for bags and the rental car, you could reach a Portland hotel around 1:15 p.m. or Camden around 2:45-3:15 p.m. Round-trip airfare for three is likely about $1,350-$1,800 in economy if booked at a reasonable lead time. A midsize rental from PWM for seven days is roughly $650-$850 before fuel.

The Boston structure would leave ORD around 8:00-9:30 a.m. and arrive around 11:15 a.m.-12:30 p.m. Rental pickup at Logan can take 60-90 minutes after landing. Driving to Portland is commonly 2 to 2.5 hours in summer traffic; Camden is closer to 3.5 hours and can run longer on Saturday. Airfare for three may land around $900-$1,350, with a seven-day Boston rental around $750-$1,000.
So Boston might save $300 or $400 on flights but give some of it back on the car.

Correct. Using midpoint estimates, PWM is about $1,575 for flights plus $750 for the car, or $2,325. Boston is about $1,125 plus $875 for the car, or $2,000. Add approximately $35-$50 more fuel and tolls to the Boston option, leaving a likely net savings near $275. At the edges of the ranges, Boston could save more, but it could also be nearly even if the rental is expensive.
What does that do to the first and last days? I do not want to count a day as coastal time if most of it is airport and interstate.

With PWM, the arrival day remains usable. If Portland is first, you should have the afternoon and dinner there. If you drive directly to Camden, you should still have late afternoon and evening on the midcoast. On departure day, a late-afternoon PWM flight would preserve breakfast and part of the morning, with a roughly two-hour drive from Camden including rental return buffer.

With Boston, arrival day is primarily transit. Even if everything runs smoothly, Portland would be an early-to-mid-afternoon arrival and Camden likely 4:30-6:00 p.m. The return is more restrictive: from Camden, I would allow at least five hours from departure to flight time for the drive, fuel, rental return, shuttle, and airport security. A 4:00 p.m. flight means leaving Camden around 11:00 a.m., earlier if traffic looks poor.
Now compare the hotel setup. Start with four nights in Portland and three in Camden, but tell me whether that is too much Portland.

Four Portland and three Camden works, though it emphasizes the city. It gives you three full Portland-based days, plus the arrival afternoon. One of those days could cover Cape Elizabeth and nearby beaches. The transfer to Camden takes about two hours without stops, or most of a day if you use it for Boothbay Harbor, Wiscasset, or Pemaquid. You then have two full midcoast days before departure.

For a family of three in July, four Portland nights in a central hotel with parking are likely $1,600-$2,200 including taxes but before parking. Three Camden or Rockland nights are roughly $1,050-$1,500. Combined lodging would be around $2,650-$3,700, plus approximately $120-$180 in Portland parking.
What about three nights Portland and four on the coast? That sounds more balanced.

Three Portland and four midcoast nights gives you the arrival afternoon and two complete Portland days, then three full midcoast days after the transfer. It is the stronger structure if the coast is the main purpose of the trip. Estimated lodging is about $1,200-$1,650 in Portland and $1,400-$2,000 around Camden or Rockland, for a similar total of $2,600-$3,650. Portland parking would likely be $90-$135 for three nights. Many midcoast inns include parking, though that needs verification property by property.
And the one-base version would mean Portland, I assume. Seven nights in Camden would make the city portion awkward.

Portland is the more functional single base, but it weakens the midcoast portion. Portland to Camden is about 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours each way in normal conditions. A Camden day trip therefore consumes nearly four hours in the car, and doing Rockland, Camden, and nearby peninsulas over multiple days becomes repetitive driving. Seven central Portland nights would likely run $2,800-$3,850 plus $210-$315 in parking. A less central property with included parking might reduce the total to roughly $2,300-$3,100, but you would trade away walkability and still face the midcoast drive.
Could Brunswick work as the single base instead?

Brunswick is the geographic compromise: about 35-45 minutes to Portland and roughly 1 hour 15 minutes to Camden. It reduces the long midcoast day but turns every Portland visit into a drive with parking. Seven nights there may be around $2,100-$2,900 with parking often included. It works if you want day trips in several directions, but it does not provide the evening experience of staying in either Portland or Camden. You would also spend roughly seven to ten hours more in the car across the week than with a split stay, depending on the itinerary.
Drop Brunswick, then. Between the airports, does a split stay make Boston any easier? We could put Portland at the beginning or the end.

A split helps, especially if Portland is last. The cleanest Boston sequence is four nights around Camden, then three nights in Portland. On arrival Saturday, drive Logan to Camden once and accept that day as transit. The move south can be a sightseeing day. On the final Saturday, Portland to Logan is usually about two hours, but I would still leave four to four and a half hours before departure because summer traffic and the rental return are variable.

Putting Portland first makes arrival easier, but the final trip from Camden to Logan is the most stressful drive of the week. For PWM, either order works. Portland first gives the easiest arrival; Camden first followed by Portland gives the easiest departure.

I would rather not build the whole return day around reaching Logan. Keep both airport options alive, but favor Portland airport. For lodging, use three Portland nights and four Camden-area nights. Is Camden itself meaningfully more expensive than Rockland?

Usually, yes. In peak summer, comparable Camden rooms can run about $50-$120 more per night because of the harbor setting and walkable village location. Four nights in Camden are likely $1,600-$2,200; Rockland is more often $1,300-$1,800. Rockland also has more practical parking and dining choices, while Camden puts you closer to the harbor and trail access around Camden Hills. A Rockport property can split the difference, but room inventory is thinner.

Owen will be twelve, so we need an actual sleeping setup for three, not a king room that merely says it allows three guests. Use either two queens or a king plus a real sofa bed when we search. For now, give me the two complete trip structures and your conclusion.

Option 1, favored: Fly nonstop ORD-PWM Saturday morning, collect the car, and stay three nights in Portland followed by four nights in Camden, Rockport, or Rockland. Return from PWM the following Saturday. Estimated flights and car: $2,000-$2,650. Lodging: $2,500-$3,850 depending mainly on the midcoast town and room type. Parking: about $90-$135 in Portland and likely included on the midcoast. Total planning range before food, fuel, and activities: approximately $4,590-$6,635. This structure preserves the arrival afternoon, provides two full Portland days and three full midcoast days, and keeps the departure drive manageable.

Option 2, lower-cost possibility: Fly nonstop ORD-BOS Saturday morning, drive directly to the Camden area for four nights, then move to Portland for three nights and return via Logan. Estimated flights and car: $1,650-$2,350. Lodging and parking are similar, with another $35-$50 in fuel and tolls. Total planning range: about $4,275-$6,385. It may save roughly $250-$400, but arrival day is mostly lost and the final drive to Logan carries more traffic risk.

My conclusion is to search PWM first and retain Boston only as a price benchmark. For lodging, the three-night Portland/four-night midcoast split is materially better than one base. The next search should compare central Portland hotels and Camden, Rockport, and Rockland properties with verified two-queen rooms or a king plus a genuine sofa bed. Nothing has been reserved.
